title: Brackets With Wildcard Stars
statement:
You get a string s made of (, ) and *. Each * is a wildcard: you may turn it into (, into ), or delete it. Each star is chosen separately.

Return true if some choice for the stars makes the string balanced: every ( is closed by a later ), and no ) appears without an open ( before it. An empty string counts as balanced.

examples.why: Delete the first two stars and close with the third: "(())". Stars can play different roles in the same string.
The counts look fine: two "(" against one ")" plus one star. But the last "(" has nothing after it that could close it. Order matters, not just counts.
The first star opens for the ")", the last star closes the "(": "()()". A rule that turns every star into the same bracket fails here.

hints: Without stars you would track one number: how many brackets are open. With stars, that number is not fixed. What do you know about it instead?
After each character, the possible open counts form a range [low, high]. How does each character move the two ends? Counts below zero are dead and can be dropped.
low counts every star as ")" and high counts every star as "(". If high drops below zero, fail. Clamp low at zero. At the end, the answer is whether low is zero.

explain.intuition:
Without stars you would keep one counter of open brackets. With stars, keep the set of open counts some choice could give. That is the DP: after each character, every count either moves by +1 ((), by −1 ()), or by any of −1, 0, +1 (*), and negative counts are thrown away because a ) with nothing open can never be repaired. It works, but the set can hold n values, so it is O(n²).

The greedy observation: the set is always a range with no holes. Start with {0}. Moving a range by −1, 0 and +1 and taking the union gives a range again; dropping negatives cuts off one end. So two numbers describe it: low (treat every star as )) and high (treat every star as (). If high goes negative, even the most generous choice has too many closers, so fail. Clamping low at zero just removes dead choices. The string can be balanced exactly when 0 is in the final range, which means low == 0.

The two-stack version works by exchange: match each ) with a real ( if one is open, and spend a star only otherwise. At the end, pair each leftover ( with a star that comes after it. Using a real ( first never hurts, because a star is at least as flexible as a ( in every later situation.
steps: On (: both go up by 1. On ): both go down by 1. On *: low goes down, high goes up.
If high < 0, return false: too many ) even if every star opens.
If low < 0, set it to 0: the choices that went negative are dead.
pitfalls: Comparing counts only. "(*)(" has enough stars to cover the difference, but the last ( is never closed.
Not clamping low at zero. On "(*)", low would end at −1 and you would wrongly return false.
In the two-stack version, pairing leftover ( with any leftover star. The star must come after the bracket: "*(" is false.

complexity.space: O(1) for the range, O(n) for two stacks

solutions.title: Set of possible open counts
solutions.idea: Track every open count some choice could produce. Each character shifts the set; counts below zero are dropped. Balanced if 0 survives.

solutions.title: Two stacks of positions
solutions.idea: Close each ) with an open ( if possible, else with a star. At the end, every leftover ( needs a star that comes after it.

solutions.title: Range of open counts
solutions.idea: The possible open counts always form a range. Track its two ends: low treats stars as ), high treats them as (. Clamp low at 0; fail if high goes negative.

followups: Return one actual assignment of the stars that balances the string.
The string now has two bracket kinds, ( ) and [ ], and a star can become any of the four or vanish. Why does the range trick stop working?
